newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court stops death-row inmate's execution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court stops death-row inmate's execution.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday granted a last-minute emergency plea to stop the execution of Virginia death-row inmate Joseph O'Dell, whose case has been championed by capital punishment foes and Pope John Paul II.
The high court issued a temporary stay of execution for O'Dell, who claimed new DNA evidence cast doubt on his murder conviction, until it acts on his appeal challenging his conviction and sentence.
O'Dell, convicted in 1986 of raping and murdering 44-year-old secretary Helen Schartner, had been scheduled to die by lethal injection on Wednesday night.

His case sparked a plea for clemency from the Vatican, street protests in Rome, where it has been widely publicised, and visits by famed death penalty opponent Sister Helen Prejean, author of the book "Dead Man Walking."
It was not known when the Supreme Court would decide O'Dell's appeal but the earliest would be in January, when the nine justices return from a three-week recess.

Asked if the public appeals by the Pope and capital punishment foes had made a difference, Robert Smith, one of O'Dell's attorneys, said, "I think the Supreme Court knows a strong legal case when it sees it and would have granted a stay even if there hadn't been one line of publicity."
Smith said in an interview with Reuters Television at his office in New York that he called O'Dell after hearing about the stay of execution and left a message for him.
He said O'Dell was doing "very well considering. It's a stressful thing. I felt like I'd been reprieved when I got the news this morning so you can imagine how he felt."

Death penalty opponents around the world have pleaded O'Dell's case, arguing that new DNA evidence shows that blood stains found on his shirt, which were used against him at his trial, do not match those of the victim.

In appealing to the Supreme Court, his lawyers said the DNA evidence raised serious questions, undermining the conviction and showing he may be innocent. They want a full hearing to consider the evidence.

"It is highly unlikely that any jury would have convicted O'Dell had it known what the DNA evidence shows," they said in asking the high court to hear the case. "O'Dell was wrongly convicted of committing this crime," the lawyers said, urging the justices to correct "this important error."
They also argued the death sentence should be overturned on the grounds the jury should have been told that O'Dell would be ineligible for parole because of his long criminal history.
Virginia Attorney General James Gilmore, rejecting O'Dell's claim of innocence, urged the high court to deny the appeal.

The court said in a one-paragraph order that the stay of execution will automatically end if it rejects Odell's appeal or when it issues a ruling if it decides to hear the appeal. If they agree to hear the appeal the case would be scheduled for oral arguments early next year, with a decision due by the end of the court's term in June.

O'Dell and his supporters have also submitted a plea for clemency to Virginia Gov. George Allen, who said in a brief statement that he will await future Supreme Court action before continuing his own "examination and deliberations."
